# Statistical Analysis Plans {#sec-analysis-plan}

A trial registers one primary outcome and publishes another. The
paper reads well, its p-value is small, and nothing in it reveals
the switch, because the only evidence is a document the reader never
opens. When the COMPare project checked every trial published over
six weeks in five high-impact medical journals against its protocol
or registry entry, 58 of 67 had discrepancies, and the papers added
a mean of 5.4 outcomes per trial that had never been declared
[@goldacre2019compare]. Most of the correction letters the team
sent went unpublished. What caught the switches was not peer review
but a dated plan to compare against; this chapter is about writing
that plan so that it binds, and so that a reader can check it did.

::: {.bookepigraph}

\begin{flushright}\small
```

significant' evidence consistent with any hypothesis.*

[Joseph P. Simmons, Leif D. Nelson, and Uri
Simonsohn]{.smallcaps}, *False-Positive Psychology*,
Psychological Science (2011)

\end{flushright}
```

**You'll be able to.**

- State a trial's estimand by its five attributes and choose a

- Draft a statistical analysis plan (SAP) whose sections map to the
  published guideline, specific enough that a second analyst would
  produce the same result.
- Compute and report a sample size with base R, apply the attrition
  assumption, and show power across a range of sample sizes.
- Tag the SAP before data access, and label every result in the
  paper as pre-specified or exploratory.

## Why pre-specify {#sec-analysis-plan-why}

The SAP is the professional biostatistician's most important
non-code document, and the argument for it is narrower and stronger
than the one usually made. It is not primarily a defense against
dishonesty. Very few analysts set out to select the analysis that
gives the answer they wanted. What they do, having looked at the
data, is make a long series of small and individually defensible
choices. Each is one they would have made differently had the data
looked otherwise, and none is experienced as a choice at all. The
p-value that emerges at the end has a nominal Type I error rate that
assumes none of this happened.

### Researcher degrees of freedom

With many possible analyses (which covariates, which
transformations, which subgroups, which outcome), the chance that
*some* analysis gives $p < 0.05$ under the null is much greater than
5%. @simmons2011false calculate that four common degrees of freedom
together inflate the false-positive rate from 5% to about 60%. The
problem does not need conscious p-hacking: in the 'garden of forking
paths' [@gelman2013garden], the reported test's calibration depends
on the choices that *would* have been made on different data, even
if the analyst made only one.

The inflation is easy to see. The simulation below generates trials
with no treatment effect at all, and lets the analyst make up to four
yes-or-no choices: which of two correlated outcomes, whether to
adjust for age, whether to drop values more than two standard deviations from the
mean,
and whether to report the older half as a subgroup. Each choice
doubles the number of analyses, and the analyst reports the smallest
p-value.

```{r}
#| label: sap-forking-sim
set.seed(20260423)

one_null_trial <- function(n = 80) {
  arm <- rep(0:1, length.out = n)
  age <- rnorm(n)
  y1 <- 0.3 * age + rnorm(n)
  y2 <- 0.5 * y1 + sqrt(0.75) * rnorm(n)
  forks <- expand.grid(outcome = 1:2, adjust = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                       trim = c(FALSE, TRUE), older = c(FALSE, TRUE))
  vapply(seq_len(nrow(forks)), \(i) {
    f <- forks[i, ]
    y <- if (f$outcome == 1) y1 else y2
    keep <- (!f$trim | abs(y - mean(y)) < 2 * sd(y)) &
      (!f$older | age > 0)
    fit <- if (f$adjust) lm(y ~ arm + age, subset = keep)
           else lm(y ~ arm, subset = keep)
    summary(fit)$coefficients["arm", 4]
  }, numeric(1))
}

pvals <- replicate(1000, one_null_trial())

# expand.grid varies the first fork fastest, so the first 2^k rows
# are every analysis available after k choices
forking <- data.frame(choices = 0:4, analyses = 2^(0:4))
forking$false_positive <- vapply(
  forking$analyses,
  \(a) mean(apply(pvals[seq_len(a), , drop = FALSE], 2, min) < 0.05),
  numeric(1)
)
forking
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sap-forking
#| fig-cap: "False-positive rate under a true null as yes-or-no
#|   analytic choices accumulate, from 1,000 simulated trials. The
#|   dashed line is the nominal 5%."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart with the number of analytic choices, 0 to 4,
#|   on the horizontal axis and the false-positive rate on the
#|   vertical axis. The rate starts near 0.05 with no choices and
#|   rises steadily with each choice, ending several times higher
#|   at four choices; a dashed horizontal line marks 0.05."
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 3.2
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(forking, aes(choices, false_positive)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = forking$choices,
    labels = paste0(forking$choices, "\n(", forking$analyses,
                    ifelse(forking$analyses == 1, " analysis)",
                           " analyses)")),
    expand = expansion(mult = 0.08)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Analytic choices", y = "False-positive rate") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Four modest choices, each of which an analyst could defend, take the
false-positive rate from
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * forking$false_positive[1])` to
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * forking$false_positive[5])`. A plan
written before the data are seen fixes the covariates, the model,
the missing-data strategy, and the multiple-comparison procedure,
and it is the only instrument that distinguishes the two situations
after the fact, because by then the analyst's memory of what they
would have done is not evidence. The trade-off is real:
pre-specification restricts flexibility. The flexibility it
restricts was producing inflated false-positive rates anyway.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** In the simulation, every one of the 16 analyses is a
valid test at the 5% level. Why does the reported result not have a
5% error rate?

**Answer.** Because the analyst reports the *smallest* of 16
p-values, and the minimum of several valid p-values is not a valid
p-value. Each test is calibrated on its own; the procedure 'run
several, report the best' is not, and the reader is told the error
rate of a single test. The tests are correlated (they share the
data), which is why the rate rises more slowly than
$1 - 0.95^{16}$, but it rises all the same.
:::

## Estimands: what the trial estimates {#sec-analysis-plan-estimands}

Before a plan says how to analyze, it has to say what is being
estimated. The E9(R1) addendum [@ich2019e9r1] of the International
Council for Harmonisation (ICH) calls that target
the **estimand** and asks for it to be stated by five attributes:

| Attribute | What it fixes | HF-HOME |
|---|---|---|
| Population | The patients the question is about | Adults discharged alive after a heart-failure admission who meet the eligibility criteria |
| Treatment conditions | What is compared | Assignment to home-health visits versus usual care |
| Variable | What is measured on each patient | Readmission or death within 30 days of discharge |
| Intercurrent events | Events after randomization that change what the variable means, and the strategy for each | Missed visit, home health outside the protocol, death |
| Population-level summary | How the variable is compared between conditions | Marginal risk difference, usual care minus home health |

: The five estimand attributes, with the HF-HOME choices from its
SAP (@sec-analysis-plan-worked). {#tbl-estimand-attributes}

### Intercurrent events and their strategies

*Intercurrent events* are 'events occurring after treatment
initiation that affect either the interpretation or the existence
of the measurements associated with the clinical question of
interest' [@ich2019e9r1]. In HF-HOME, a home-health patient who
never receives the visit, a usual-care patient who gets home health
anyway, and a patient who dies before any readmission are all
intercurrent events. The addendum names five strategies for them,
and each one asks a different question:

| Strategy | Question it answers | HF-HOME example | What it requires |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treatment policy | Effect of the assigned treatment, whatever patients then received | Missed and outside-protocol visits ignored: analyzed as randomized (the SAP's choice) | Outcomes on every patient, including the nonadherent |
| Composite | The event is itself an outcome | Death before readmission counts as an event (the SAP's choice) | A variable defined for everyone |
| Hypothetical | Effect had the event not occurred | Effect had every home-health patient received the visit | A model for an unobserved scenario, with untestable assumptions |
| While on treatment | Response before the event | Readmission while home-health services were active | Comparable observation windows across arms |
| Principal stratum | Effect in patients who would (or would not) have the event | Effect among patients who would receive a visit if assigned home health | Assumptions that identify a stratum no one observes directly |

: Strategies for intercurrent events, illustrated with HF-HOME.
{#tbl-estimand-strategies}

A treatment-policy strategy cannot handle a terminal event such as
death, because no outcome exists after it; that is why HF-HOME uses
the composite strategy for death and treatment policy for the
visits. The choice determines what counts as missing data, which is
why @sec-missing-trials starts from the estimand.

### Why 'patients who got the visit' answers no question

The tempting analysis compares patients by what they received. The
running study's files show how far that drifts from any estimand:

```{r}
#| label: sap-estimand-receipt
#| message: false
library(dplyr)

hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
read_hf <- function(file) {
  readr::read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, file),
                  col_types = readr::cols(patient_id = "c",
                                          .default = "?"))
}

hf_rand <- read_hf("randomization.csv")
visited <- read_hf("visits.csv") |>
  filter(visit_type == "home_health", visit_day <= 7) |>
  distinct(patient_id) |>
  mutate(visit_7d = TRUE)

hf <- hf_rand |>
  select(patient_id, arm) |>
  left_join(visited, by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  left_join(read_hf("outcomes.csv") |>
              select(patient_id, event_30d, days_to_event),
            by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one",
            unmatched = "error") |>
  mutate(visit_7d = coalesce(visit_7d, FALSE),
         arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health")))
stopifnot(nrow(hf) == nrow(hf_rand))

hf |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarize(received_visit = round(mean(visit_7d), 3))

by_receipt <- hf |>
  filter(arm == "Home health") |>
  group_by(visit_7d) |>
  summarize(patients = n(),
            risk = round(mean(event_30d, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
            event_by_day_7 = sum(event_30d == 1 & days_to_event <= 7,
                                 na.rm = TRUE))
by_receipt
```

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**Subsetting on what patients received breaks randomization, and the
result looks like a large effect.** Within the home-health arm,
patients without a visit had a 30-day risk of
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * by_receipt$risk[!by_receipt$visit_7d])`
against
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * by_receipt$risk[by_receipt$visit_7d])`
for those visited. That is not the effect of the visit. Frail
patients were less likely to receive one, and
`r by_receipt$event_by_day_7[!by_receipt$visit_7d]` of the unvisited
had their event by day 7, which in the trial's records prevents the
visit (the immortal-time trap of @sec-team-science). A principal
stratum is defined by what a patient *would* experience, which
randomization balances; a subset defined by what patients *did*
experience is not balanced by anything.
:::

### Exercises

1. Using `outcomes.csv` and `randomization.csv`, count by arm the
   patients whose first event was death. Which strategy does the
   HF-HOME SAP apply to them, and why could it not use a
   treatment-policy strategy?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-18-estimand
deaths <- hf_rand |>
  select(patient_id, arm) |>
  left_join(read_hf("outcomes.csv") |> select(patient_id, first_event),
            by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one",
            unmatched = "error") |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarize(ascertained = sum(!is.na(first_event)),
            death_first = sum(first_event == "death", na.rm = TRUE))
deaths
```

The SAP uses a composite strategy: death within 30 days is an event,
so the variable is defined for every patient. A treatment-policy
strategy would need the readmission outcome after death, which does
not exist; the addendum notes that treatment policy cannot be
implemented for terminal events. Treating death as censoring, or
dropping the deaths, would instead estimate an effect among
survivors, a population that the treatment itself may change.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A colleague proposes a 'per-protocol' analysis of
HF-HOME restricted to home-health patients who received the visit
and usual-care patients who did not. Which estimand does it target?

**Answer.** None of the five. It is neither a hypothetical estimand
(that needs a model for what unvisited patients would have
experienced) nor a principal stratum (that needs the patients who
*would* be visited if assigned, identified in both arms). It
compares two subsets selected after randomization by frailty and by
early events, so its estimate mixes the treatment effect with those
differences. If the question is the effect of actually receiving
the visit, state it as a hypothetical or principal-stratum estimand
and pre-specify the assumptions that identify it.
:::

## What a SAP contains {#sec-analysis-plan-template}

A standard biostatistical SAP has the sections in @tbl-sap-sections.
They condense the published guideline for the content of
clinical-trial SAPs [@gamble2017sap], whose 55 items are the fuller
checklist to use for a trial, and each maps to the statistical
principles in ICH E9 [@ich1998e9] and its addendum. A downloadable
SAP skeleton with these sections will accompany the book.

| SAP section | Contents | Gamble et al. (2017) | ICH E9 or E9(R1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Administrative | Version, date, revision history, signatures | Administrative information (1 to 6) | (see @sec-analysis-plan-tagging) |
| 1. Background | Why this study, in half a page | Introduction: background and rationale (7) | 2.1 Trial context |
| 2. Questions and estimands | Each question with its hypothesis and estimand | Introduction: objectives (8) | E9(R1) A.3 Estimands |
| 3. Design | Design, allocation, randomization, sample size | Study methods (9 to 15) | 3.1 Design configuration; 3.5 Sample size |
| 4. Eligibility | Inclusion and exclusion, each testable from data | Trial population: eligibility (22) | 2.2.1 Population |
| 5. Primary outcome | Data fields, time window, transformation | Analysis: outcome definitions (26) | 2.2.2 Primary and secondary variables |
| 6. Secondary outcomes | Same level of detail | Analysis: outcome definitions (26) | 2.2.2 |
| 7. Covariates | Each named, with coding and reference level | Analysis: analysis methods (27) | 5.7 Subgroups, interactions and covariates |
| 8. Primary analysis | Model, estimator, interval, Type I error, analysis set | Analysis methods (27); analysis populations (20) | 5.2 Analysis sets; 5.5 Estimation, confidence intervals and hypothesis testing |
| 9. Secondary analyses | Each with the same detail | Analysis: analysis methods (27) | 5.5 |
| 10. Sensitivity analyses | Each a named departure from a stated assumption | Analysis: analysis methods (27) | E9(R1) A.5.2 Sensitivity analysis |
| 11. Missing data | Assumed mechanism, primary method, diagnostics | Analysis: missing data (28) | 5.3 Missing values and outliers |
| 12. Multiple testing | The procedure and the family it covers | Statistical principles: confidence intervals and P values (16 to 18) | 5.6 Adjustment of significance and confidence levels |
| 13. Reporting | Tables, figures, flow diagram | Trial population (21 to 25) | VII Reporting |

: SAP sections, with their counterparts in the guideline of
@gamble2017sap (item numbers in parentheses) and ICH E9 (section
numbers). {#tbl-sap-sections}

Not every section is needed for every study. For an observational
secondary analysis, sections 3 and 4 are simpler, and sections 8 to
12 are the same.

### Specific enough to constrain

A SAP that says 'we will fit a regression model' has specified
nothing. One that says 'multivariable logistic regression of 30-day
readmission or death on randomized arm (home health vs. usual care),
adjusted for age (continuous), sex, ejection fraction (continuous),
and discharge medication count (continuous), with a 5% Type I error
rate, two-sided' has constrained the researcher degrees of freedom
that matter. Aim for the second.

Where you do not know whether an assumption will hold, pre-specify a
method that remains valid either way rather than a test that chooses
between methods. 'If the residuals show heteroscedasticity, we will
use heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC1) standard errors; otherwise
classical standard errors (SEs)' looks careful but
is a pretest procedure: the combined rule's error rate is that of
neither branch, and classical SEs chosen after a heteroscedasticity
test that lacked power are the worst of both. 'We will use HC3
standard errors' commits to an estimator that is valid whether or
not the variance is constant and costs little when it is
[@long2000hc]. 'We will use SEs' constrains nothing.

### Complete is not the same as good

The template says what a SAP must contain, not whether the analysis
it specifies is a good one; a SAP can be complete, tagged before
data access, and still pre-specify a weak analysis. Harrell's author
checklist [@harrell2024checklist], written for the reviewer of a
finished manuscript, is the right instrument to run against a draft,
because every item on it is a way a paper gets rejected that a plan
could have prevented. Its recurring targets are decisions sections 7
and 8 invite: categorizing a continuous covariate rather than
modeling it with a spline, selecting variables stepwise, reporting a
p-value without the interval that gives it magnitude, and choosing a
sample size from an effect observed in a previous study rather than
the effect worth detecting. *Regression Modeling Strategies*
[@harrell2015rms] is the book-length argument behind those items.
Read the checklist once before you draft section 8, and again after.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A draft SAP says: 'Missing data will be handled
appropriately, with sensitivity analyses as needed.' Which sections
of @tbl-sap-sections does it fail, and what would fix it?

**Answer.** Sections 10 and 11. It names no mechanism, no method,
and no sensitivity analysis, so any analysis chosen after the data
arrive would satisfy it. The fix states the assumed mechanism and
the variables it conditions on, the primary method (with $M$ if
imputing), and each sensitivity analysis by method and range, as in
section 11 of the HF-HOME SAP below.
:::

## Sample size {#sec-analysis-plan-power}

Base R's `stats` package covers the two designs most clinical SAPs
start from, a parallel-group randomized controlled trial (RCT) with
a continuous or a binary outcome: `power.t.test()` for a continuous outcome and
`power.prop.test()` for a binary one. Supplying `power` solves for
the sample size per arm; supplying `n` solves for power:

```{r}
#| label: sap-power-base
# parallel-group RCT, continuous outcome:
# n per arm at 80% power for a standardized effect of 0.5
power.t.test(delta = 0.5, sd = 1, power = 0.80,
             sig.level = 0.05)

# the converse question: power at 50 per arm
power.t.test(n = 50, delta = 0.5, sd = 1)$power
```

For designs beyond these, community packages such as `pwr` and, for
group-sequential and adaptive trials, `rpact` are the usual next
step. The in-house `zzpower` package is one further option. It is
installed from GitHub rather than CRAN and has not been through an
external review, so where base R covers the same design, cross-check
its answer against `stats`; for the calculation below the two agree
once rounded up to whole patients.

```{r}
#| label: sap-power-calc
#| message: false
library(zzpower)

zzpower::power_calc("ttest_2groups",
           target_power  = 0.80,
           effect_size   = 0.5,
           effect_method = "cohens_d",
           alpha         = 0.05)
```

In the SAP, report the sample size with the underlying assumptions,
and apply the attrition assumption rather than merely stating it.
The calculation gives the number of participants who must be
*analyzed*; the number enrolled has to be larger by the factor
$1/(1 - \text{attrition})$:

```{r}
#| label: sap-attrition
attrition  <- 0.10
n_analyzed <- power.t.test(delta = 0.5, sd = 1,
                           power = 0.80)$n
n_enrolled <- ceiling(n_analyzed / (1 - attrition))

c(analyzed = ceiling(n_analyzed), enrolled = n_enrolled)
```

> The study will enroll `r n_enrolled` participants per arm
> (`r 2 * n_enrolled` in total), so that with 10% attrition
> `r ceiling(n_analyzed)` per arm remain for analysis, giving 80%
> power to detect a standardized effect of 0.5 at a two-sided
> $\alpha = 0.05$.

A plan that says '64 per arm, assuming 10% attrition' and enrolls 64
has assumed the attrition and then ignored it. If the assumptions
are uncertain, show power across a range of sample sizes or effects,
as @fig-sap-power does for HF-HOME, and choose the planned size with
feasibility in view.

### Exercises

2. Use `power.t.test()` to compute the required sample size for a
   two-arm comparison under three plausible standardized effect
   sizes (small, medium, large). Then inflate each for a cluster
   randomized design with 20 patients per practice and an
   intracluster correlation of 0.02, and report the number of
   clusters required.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
**The individual-level requirement first.**

```{r}
#| label: soln-18-1
per_arm <- vapply(
  c(small = 0.2, medium = 0.5, large = 0.8),
  \(d) power.t.test(delta = d, sd = 1, power = 0.80,
                    sig.level = 0.05)$n,
  numeric(1))

ceiling(per_arm)          # analytic n per arm
```

With `sd = 1`, `delta` is the standardized effect. The same
calculation in `zzpower` reads its result from `sample_sizes` rather
than `sample_size`: the element is a list, because a two-arm
calculation returns per-arm and total figures separately, along with
an intention-to-treat (ITT) inflated version. Its `$n` is the analytic requirement per
arm, and it agrees with base R once rounded up:

```{r}
#| label: soln-18-1-zzpower
#| message: false
library(zzpower)

per_arm_zz <- vapply(
  c(small = 0.2, medium = 0.5, large = 0.8),
  \(d) power_calc("ttest_2groups",
                  target_power  = 0.80,
                  effect_size   = d,
                  effect_method = "cohens_d",
                  alpha         = 0.05)$sample_sizes$n,
  numeric(1))

stopifnot(identical(ceiling(per_arm), ceiling(per_arm_zz)))
```

The per-arm requirement is what the design effect below scales.

**Then the design effect.** A cluster randomized trial does not
randomize patients; it randomizes practices, and patients within a
practice resemble one another. The variance inflation is
$\text{DEFF} = 1 + (m - 1)\rho$, with $m$ patients per cluster and
$\rho$ the intracluster correlation:

```{r}
#| label: soln-18-1b
m   <- 20      # patients per practice
rho <- 0.02    # intracluster correlation

deff <- 1 + (m - 1) * rho

total <- 2 * per_arm                 # both arms

data.frame(
  effect       = names(per_arm),
  n_total      = ceiling(total),
  deff         = round(deff, 2),
  n_cluster    = ceiling(total * deff),
  clusters     = ceiling(ceiling(total * deff) / m),
  row.names    = NULL
)
```

An intracluster correlation of 0.02 sounds negligible and is not.
With 20 patients per practice it inflates the required sample by
38%, because the design effect depends on $\rho$ and cluster size
jointly. Doubling the cluster size to 40 would inflate it by 78%
instead, so recruiting more patients per practice buys
progressively less.

Two things belong in the SAP alongside this table. The value of
$\rho$ is an assumption, not a measurement, and it should be
attributed to a source and given a sensitivity range. And the
number that gets recruited is `clusters`, rounded up, so the
realized sample is generally larger than `n_cluster`; quoting the
latter as the target understates what the trial must enroll.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A protocol states 80% power with 750 evaluable
patients per arm, and a colleague checked the arithmetic by eye.
What is the only check that counts?

**Answer.** Recomputing it from the stated assumptions, in code, and
putting the computed number in the prose. At a 25% control risk and
a 5-point reduction, 750 per arm falls well short of 80% power, as
@sec-analysis-plan-worked computes. A typed number in a protocol is
evidence of what someone believed, not of what the design delivers
(Habit 10).
:::

## Pre-specified versus exploratory {#sec-analysis-plan-exploratory}

The distinction is about *when* an analysis was decided, and it
determines what the result can claim:

| | Pre-specified | Exploratory |
|---|---|---|
| When decided | Written in the SAP before data access | After seeing the data, or added later (a reviewer request, an unexpected finding) |
| Error rates | Calibrated to the SAP's specification | Uncalibrated |
| Authority | The full inferential authority of the study | Hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory |
| In the SAP | Listed under 'Pre-specified analyses' | Listed under 'Exploratory analyses (hypothesis-generating, reported with appropriate caution)' |
| In the paper | Methods name the SAP and its version | Labeled exploratory where reported |

: Pre-specified and exploratory analyses. {#tbl-prespecified}

In the paper, the label goes in the methods section:

> The primary analysis was a multivariable logistic regression of
> 30-day readmission or death on randomized arm, pre-specified in
> the analysis plan (Supplementary Material, version 1.0). Subgroup
> analyses by age were exploratory and are reported as
> hypothesis-generating.

The convention spares the reader from over-interpreting exploratory
findings while preserving their value as motivation for follow-up.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
Use a model to flag analyses that look exploratory, not to decide
which were pre-specified; only your timeline knows that.

> **Context.** Below are the analysis list from my draft results
> section and the list of analyses in SAP version 1.0, with the
> date of its tag and the date of data access.
>
> **Constraints.** Classify each analysis in the results as
> pre-specified (it appears in SAP v1.0 with the same outcome,
> model, population, and covariates) or exploratory (anything else).
> Treat any change of outcome, time point, covariate set, or
> analysis population as a deviation, not a match.
>
> **Criteria.** For each analysis, quote the SAP sentence it matches,
> or state 'no match'. List every SAP analysis that does not appear
> in the results.

*Failure mode.* The model matches on topic rather than
specification, calling a 90-day outcome pre-specified because the
SAP mentions 30-day readmission, and it cannot know when an analysis
was decided. *Check.* For every 'pre-specified' label, confirm that
the quoted sentence is in the tagged SAP (`git show
sap-v1.0-locked:SAP/sap-v1.0.qmd`); the list of unreported SAP
analyses is the outcome-switching audit of this chapter's opening.
A SAP and a results outline are structure, not data
(@sec-ai-governance).
:::

### Exercises

3. Locate a published trial with a publicly available SAP or
   protocol. Audit whether the paper's analyses match it: list the
   pre-specified primary and secondary outcomes, the reported ones,
   and every discrepancy, and classify each as an amendment, an
   exploratory analysis, or unreported.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
There is no single key, because the paper is yours to choose. A good
audit is a table with one row per outcome: as pre-specified (with
the document, version, and date), as reported, and the
classification. It counts the outcomes added without declaration
and the pre-specified outcomes not reported, as COMPare did
[@goldacre2019compare], and for each discrepancy checks whether the
paper itself discloses and explains it. An undisclosed switch of the
primary outcome is the finding that matters most.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You pre-specified a primary logistic regression.
Reviewers ask for a subgroup analysis by age. You run it and find a
significant interaction. How should this appear in the paper?

**Answer.** As an exploratory analysis, clearly labeled. It was not
pre-specified, and the test was selected after the data were seen,
so its Type I error rate is not 5% in any meaningful sense. Report
it as hypothesis-generating, in the discussion rather than as a
confirmatory result; it is a candidate for a future pre-registered
study. Mislabeling exploratory findings as confirmatory is among
the most common forms of inferential overreach in clinical
research.
:::

## Version control and tagging {#sec-analysis-plan-tagging}

A SAP that can be edited after the data arrive is not a
pre-specification, whatever it says on its front page. What makes
the claim checkable is a timestamped tag in a history nobody can
quietly rewrite. @fig-sap-timeline is the sequence that has to hold.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-sap-timeline
%%| fig-alt: "Left-to-right timeline. Drafting the SAP with no data
%%|   access leads to an immutable pushed git tag sap-v1.0, then to
%%|   data lock and unblinding, then to analysis, then to a report
%%|   that labels results pre-specified or exploratory. A dashed
%%|   branch from the data lock shows an amendment made after data
%%|   access, tagged sap-v1.1 and marked exploratory unless
%%|   justified and dated, rejoining the analysis."
%%| fig-cap: "The SAP against the data timeline. Everything to the
%%|   left of the lock is pre-specified and carries the study's
%%|   inferential authority. Anything written after it is
%%|   exploratory, and an amendment made after data access must be
%%|   tagged as its own version so that the order of events stays
%%|   auditable."
flowchart LR
  D["Draft SAP<br/><i>no data access</i>"]
  D --> T1["<b>git tag sap-v1.0</b><br/><i>pushed, immutable</i>"]
  T1 --> L["Data lock<br/>and unblinding"]
  L --> A["Analysis<br/><i>executes the plan</i>"]
  A --> R["Report<br/><i>labels pre-specified<br/>vs exploratory</i>"]
  L -.->|"amendment after<br/>data access"| T2["<b>git tag sap-v1.1</b><br/><i>exploratory unless<br/>justified and dated</i>"]
  T2 -.-> A
```

The SAP lives in the project's Git repository:

```
project/
├── SAP/
│   ├── sap-v1.0.qmd       # current SAP
│   ├── sap-v1.0.pdf       # rendered version submitted to ClinicalTrials.gov
│   └── amendments/
│       ├── amendment-1.qmd
│       └── amendment-2.qmd
└── ...
```

Tag the moment of data lock, and push the tag:

```bash
git tag -a sap-v1.0-locked -m "SAP locked at data access 2026-04-23"
git push origin sap-v1.0-locked
```

Later amendments are separate commits and tags:

```bash
git tag -a sap-v1.1-amendment-1 -m "Amendment 1: revised missing-data strategy following blinded data review"
```

Amendments must be made before unblinded data analysis to retain
confirmatory status; amendments made after unblinding (after seeing
outcomes) are exploratory by definition. For trials, deposit the
locked SAP at the trial registry (ClinicalTrials.gov, ANZCTR,
ISRCTN) at the time of registration. The deposited copy is the
authoritative pre-specification.

### Exercises

4. In a scratch repository, commit a one-page SAP and tag it
   `sap-v1.0-locked`. Write an amendment that revises the
   missing-data strategy after a blinded data review, commit it, and
   tag it `sap-v1.1-amendment-1`. Show that the order of events is
   auditable.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
The evidence is in Git's own records (display-only; run in your
scratch repository):

```bash
git tag -n1 --sort=creatordate
git log --format='%h %ad %s' --date=iso -- SAP/
git diff sap-v1.0-locked sap-v1.1-amendment-1 -- SAP/
```

The first lists both tags with their messages in creation order;
the second dates every change to the SAP; the third shows exactly
what the amendment changed. Locally these prove *what* and *in what
order*, not *when*: a determined author could have created both
tags yesterday. Pushing the tags, and depositing the SAP with a
registry, is what supplies credible dates (see the Check below).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** You tag the SAP `sap-v1.0` before data lock. A
skeptical reviewer points out that `git tag` can be created at any
time with any name, and that you could have written the tag last
week after seeing the results. What actually stops you?

**Answer.** Locally, nothing. The reviewer is right about the
mechanism and wrong about the conclusion. A tag is a label on a
commit and can be created, deleted, and moved at will, and commit
dates are metadata a determined person can set. A repository on
your laptop proves *what*, not *when*.

What supplies the timing is publication to somewhere you do not
control. Pushing the tag to a remote creates a record on a server
with its own timestamps and log. The registry deposit is stronger
still, since ClinicalTrials.gov records a submission date you cannot
edit, and stronger again is anything that timestamps content
cryptographically, such as a Zenodo digital object identifier (DOI) or a registration
on the Open Science Framework (OSF). The
tag makes the pre-specification *findable and unambiguous*; an
external record makes it *credible*. A SAP tagged but never pushed
provides organization without evidence. This is the same
distinction @sec-federal draws between hosting an artifact and
depositing it.
:::

## Worked example: the HF-HOME SAP {#sec-analysis-plan-worked}

The design numbers in the plan below are computed, not typed, from
four assumptions: a 25% event rate under usual care, a 5-point
absolute reduction worth detecting, 80% power at two-sided
$\alpha = 0.05$, and up to 10% of patients without an ascertainable
outcome.

```{r}
#| label: sap-hfhome-n
p_usual    <- 0.25
p_home     <- 0.20
missing_hf <- 0.10

hf_design <- power.prop.test(p1 = p_usual, p2 = p_home,
                             power = 0.80)
n_eval    <- ceiling(hf_design$n)
n_rand    <- ceiling(hf_design$n / (1 - missing_hf))
or_hf     <- (p_home / (1 - p_home)) /
  (p_usual / (1 - p_usual))
power_750 <- power.prop.test(n = 750, p1 = p_usual,
                             p2 = p_home)$power

c(evaluable_per_arm  = n_eval,
  randomized_per_arm = n_rand,
  randomized_total   = 2 * n_rand)
round(c(odds_ratio = or_hf, power_at_750 = power_750), 2)
```

The last line is a warning about typed numbers. An earlier draft of
this plan read '1500 (750 per arm) for 80% power to detect OR = 0.75
at baseline rate 0.25'. At those rates 750 per arm gives
`r round(100 * power_750)`% power, not 80%, and no one checking the
prose by eye would have noticed. @fig-sap-power shows where the two
numbers sit on the design's power curve.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sap-power
#| fig-cap: "Power of the HF-HOME design (25% versus 20% risk,
#|   two-sided alpha 0.05) against evaluable patients per arm. The
#|   earlier draft's 750 per arm falls well short of the 80% line;
#|   the computed requirement meets it."
#| fig-alt: "Rising power curve from about 0.4 at 400 patients per
#|   arm to above 0.9 at 1,600. A dashed horizontal line marks 80%
#|   power. Two vertical lines mark 750 per arm, where the curve is
#|   near 0.64, and the computed requirement of about 1,094 per arm,
#|   where it crosses 0.80."
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 3.2
power_curve <- data.frame(n = seq(400, 1600, by = 10))
power_curve$power <- power.prop.test(n = power_curve$n, p1 = p_usual,
                                     p2 = p_home)$power
marks <- data.frame(n = c(750, n_eval),
                    label = c("750 (earlier draft)",
                              paste(format(n_eval, big.mark = ","),
                                    "(computed)")))

ggplot(power_curve, aes(n, power)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = 2) +
  geom_vline(data = marks, aes(xintercept = n), color = "grey40") +
  geom_text(data = marks, aes(x = n, y = 0.42, label = label),
            angle = 90, hjust = 0, vjust = -0.5, size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Evaluable patients per arm", y = "Power") +
  theme_minimal()
```

> **Title:** Statistical Analysis Plan for the
> Effect of Post-Discharge Home Health Visits on
> 30-Day Readmission or Death in Heart Failure
> (HF-HOME-RCT)
>
> **Version:** 1.0, locked 2026-04-23.
>
> ## 1. Background
>
> Patients hospitalized with heart failure have a
> 30-day risk of readmission or death of about 25%. Home-health visits
> within 7 days of discharge have been associated
> with reduced readmission in observational studies
> [...]. We test the causal effect with a parallel-
> group RCT.
>
> ## 2. Research question and estimand
>
> Among adults discharged alive after a heart-failure
> admission, does assignment to a home-health
> program (at least one visit within 7 days of
> discharge), compared with usual care, reduce the
> 30-day risk of readmission or death? The estimand,
> by its five ICH E9(R1) attributes
> [@ich2019e9r1]:
>
> - *Population:* patients meeting section 4.
> - *Treatment conditions:* assignment to the
>   home-health program versus usual care.
> - *Variable:* all-cause readmission or death
>   within 30 days of index discharge (section 5).
> - *Intercurrent events:* death before readmission
>   is handled by a composite strategy (it is an
>   event), so the variable is defined for every
>   patient. Not receiving the visit in the
>   home-health arm, and receiving home health
>   outside the protocol in the usual-care arm, are
>   handled by a treatment-policy strategy: patients
>   are analyzed as randomized, whatever they
>   received.
> - *Population-level summary:* the marginal risk
>   difference, usual care minus home health, so
>   that a positive value is a reduction.
>
> ## 3. Design
>
> Parallel-group, individually randomized, open-
> label RCT. 1:1 allocation. Stratified by site and
> baseline ejection fraction.
>
> ## 4. Eligibility
>
> Inclusion: (a) admitted with primary diagnosis
> heart failure (ICD-10 I50.x); (b) age $\geq 18$;
> (c) discharged alive.
> Exclusion: (a) hospice; (b) inability to consent;
> (c) prior enrollment in this trial.
>
> ## 5. Primary outcome
>
> Binary: all-cause readmission or death within 30
> days of index discharge. Readmission is any
> inpatient admission to any institution. Source:
> institutional EHR linked to the state HIE and to
> state death records.
>
> ## 8. Primary analysis
>
> Logistic regression of the primary outcome on
> randomized arm (as randomized, never as treatment
> received), adjusted for age (continuous), sex,
> ejection fraction (continuous), discharge
> medication count (continuous), and site (fixed
> effect, as a stratification factor). The arm
> coefficient of this model is a *conditional* odds
> ratio and is not the estimand. The estimand is
> obtained by standardization (g-computation):
> predict each randomized patient's risk under each
> arm, average over all randomized patients, and
> take the difference. 95% CI by nonparametric
> bootstrap (2,000 resamples, percentile). Two-sided
> $\alpha = 0.05$. The conditional odds ratio is
> reported as a supportive summary, labeled as
> conditional.
>
> Sample size: `r format(n_eval, big.mark = ",")`
> evaluable patients per arm give 80% power to
> detect a reduction from `r 100 * p_usual`% to
> `r 100 * p_home`% (odds ratio
> `r sprintf("%.2f", or_hf)`) at two-sided
> $\alpha = 0.05$ (`power.prop.test`). Allowing for
> up to `r 100 * missing_hf`% of patients without an
> ascertainable outcome, we randomize
> `r format(n_rand, big.mark = ",")` per arm
> (`r format(2 * n_rand, big.mark = ",")` in total).
>
> ## 11. Missing data
>
> Outcome: missing only for patients who cannot be
> linked to the state HIE (for example, after moving
> out of state). Primary: the standardized estimator
> of section 8, fitted to patients with an
> ascertained outcome and averaged over all
> randomized patients, which is valid if
> missingness is independent of the outcome given
> arm and the adjustment covariates. Sensitivity:
> delta-adjustment tipping-point analysis. In the
> home-health arm, unascertained patients are
> assigned a risk $\delta$ times that of their
> observed peers, with $\delta$ increased from 1
> until the 95% CI includes zero; in the usual-care
> arm they are assigned the observed risk. Missing
> patients stay in the denominator. Covariates:
> $<5\%$ missing expected; imputed by the pooled
> mean (continuous) or mode (categorical), which is
> valid for baseline covariates in a randomized
> trial.
>
> ## 12. Multiple testing
>
> Primary outcome at two-sided $\alpha = 0.05$.
> Secondary outcomes by a fixed-sequence
> (hierarchical) procedure, in this order:
> (S1) 30-day all-cause readmission alone;
> (S2) 30-day emergency department visit;
> (S3) 90-day readmission or death. Each is tested
> at $\alpha = 0.05$ only if the primary and every
> earlier secondary test rejected; at the first
> non-rejection testing stops, and the remaining
> outcomes are reported as estimates with CIs and
> no p-value. This controls the familywise error
> rate at 0.05 across the primary and secondary
> outcomes. Testing the primary at 0.05 and the
> secondaries at Bonferroni-corrected levels
> regardless of the primary result does not: the
> two families each spend 0.05, and the familywise
> rate can approach 0.10.

This level of specificity is what 'pre-specified' means. Vagueness
invites researcher degrees of freedom.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
The running study's randomization file was generated from this
plan, so the randomized count per arm should equal the SAP's
computed `n_rand`:

```{r}
#| label: sap-hfhome-verify
table(hf_rand$arm)
stopifnot(all(table(hf_rand$arm) == n_rand))
```
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
> **Context.** I am drafting sections 2 and 8 of a SAP for a
> two-arm randomized trial. Attached: the protocol synopsis
> (population, interventions, outcome definition, visit schedule)
> and the design assumptions (control risk, effect worth
> detecting, power, $\alpha$, expected unascertained fraction).
>
> **Constraints.** State the estimand by all five ICH E9(R1)
> attributes, naming each intercurrent event and its strategy.
> Specify the primary estimator and say whether its summary is
> marginal or conditional. Compute the sample size with
> `power.prop.test()` and show the code; inflate for the
> unascertained fraction.
>
> **Criteria.** Every attribute is present and specific enough to
> compute from the data dictionary; the population-level summary
> matches the estimator; the sample-size code runs and reproduces
> the stated number.

*Failure mode.* The draft lists 'ITT population' in place of the
estimand, calls the adjusted odds ratio 'the treatment effect' when
the summary is a marginal risk difference, or quotes a sample size
from memory that the code does not reproduce; this chapter's own
earlier draft was underpowered in exactly that way. *Check.* Run the
code; compare every attribute with @tbl-estimand-attributes; confirm
that the estimator's output is the summary the estimand names.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 5: pre-specify, then tag.** Write the estimand and the
   analysis before data access, tag the SAP, and push the tag.
2. **Habit 10: every number in the prose is computed.** The
   sample size, the power, and the odds ratio in the SAP come from
   code, which is how the 750-per-arm error was caught.
3. **Habit 3: version control from day one.** An amendment is a new
   commit and a new tag, so that the order of plan and data stays
   auditable.

## Cumulative practice

5. *Cumulative (uses @sec-git-solo and @sec-missing).* Draft a SAP
   skeleton for a hypothetical cluster randomized trial of a
   patient-education intervention, with every section of
   @tbl-sap-sections. State the estimand by its five attributes,
   include the cluster sample-size table from exercise 2, write
   section 11 with a named primary assumption and two sensitivity
   analyses, and commit and tag it in a repository.
6. *On your own work (no key).* Take an analysis you completed
   without a SAP and write the retrospective SAP that should have
   preceded it. Mark each choice that was made after seeing the
   data, and label the results that depend on those choices as
   exploratory.

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code or rule | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| State the estimand | Population, treatment, variable, intercurrent events with strategy, summary | Analyzing toward an unstated target |
| Sample size, binary outcome | `power.prop.test(p1, p2, power = 0.80)` | Typed, unchecked sample sizes |
| Sample size, continuous | `power.t.test(delta, sd, power = 0.80)` | The same |
| Power at a planned size | `power.prop.test(n = 750, p1, p2)$power` | An underpowered design |
| Apply attrition | `ceiling(n / (1 - attrition))` | Stating attrition and enrolling as if none |
| Standard errors | Pre-specify HC3, not a pretest | A combined rule with unknown error rate |
| Multiplicity | Fixed-sequence or Holm, with the family named | Familywise error near 0.10 |
| Lock the plan | `git tag -a sap-v1.0-locked`, then `git push origin` the tag | An undatable plan |
| Label results | Pre-specified or exploratory, in methods | Exploratory findings read as confirmatory |

: Analysis plans at a glance. {#tbl-sap-cheat-sheet}

## Further reading

- [@gamble2017sap], the consensus guideline on what a clinical-trial
  SAP must contain; its 55 items are the full checklist behind
  @tbl-sap-sections.
- [@ich2019e9r1], the ICH E9(R1) addendum on estimands and
  sensitivity analysis, with its parent guideline [@ich1998e9].
- [@harrell2024checklist], the shortest useful audit of a draft
  SAP's analysis sections.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-18}

1. The SAP locks in the analysis plan before data access, so that
   the eventual published results reflect hypotheses formed in
   advance rather than post-hoc choices made in the light of the
   data. It limits the 'garden of forking paths' that would
   otherwise inflate Type I error and enable p-hacking. Federally
   funded trials require it; confirmatory analyses in any setting
   benefit from it.
2. (Any five of:) background and rationale; research questions,
   hypotheses, and estimands; study design and sample size;
   inclusion/exclusion criteria; primary outcome definition;
   secondary outcomes; covariates; primary analysis; secondary
   analyses; sensitivity analyses; missing-data handling;
   multiple-testing procedure; reporting plan.
3. Pre-specified analyses represent commitments made before data
   access; they carry the full inferential authority of the study's
   design. Exploratory analyses are generated after seeing the
   data; they are hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory, and
   should be reported with appropriate caution. Conflating the two
   misleads readers about the evidential strength of the findings
   and is one of the most common sources of reproducibility failure
   in biomedical research.
